entries.subject: Add release notes: a customer view and a technical admin view
paragraphs: The changelog had gone stale — it still ended at 2026-08-02 while a month of work shipped behind it, because keeping it current depended on somebody remembering. Two audiences needed different things from it, so there are now two views over one timeline, reachable from a new button in the top bar.

What's new (/whats-new) is for customers and the people who work with us: curated, plain-language, grouped by month, filterable by New / Improved / Foundation. It shares its source with the public /changelog, so the two can no longer drift apart. A dot on the top-bar button marks anything shipped since this browser last looked.

Admin -> Releases (/admin/releases) is for people with backend access: every change that landed on main, with the date and time, who shipped it, the commit body explaining WHY, the areas touched, file and line counts, and — called out in orange — any database migrations the change carried, because those have to be applied to a self-hosted install before the change works. Searchable and filterable by category, and each entry expands rather than dumping a diff.

The admin half is generated from git history (npm run notes:build), not written, so it cannot fall behind what is deployed. A CI job regenerates and commits it on every push to main, which is what makes the feed correspond to merges instead of to good intentions. The page states which commit it was generated from against the commit actually running, so "is this current?" is answerable rather than assumed.

The customer notes stay hand-written on purpose: a commit subject is not release copy, and most of what we ship is noise to someone using the product. To keep that from going stale again, the admin page counts how many changes have shipped since the last customer note and says so in amber until somebody writes one. It is at zero now — the September work is written up.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Upgrade Next.js to 16.3.5 and clear every dependency advisory
paragraphs: Adding a dependency scan for the launch checklist's Security item turned up 22 advisories on the running product, including two CRITICAL unauthenticated remote-code-execution issues in Next.js — one on Windows-hosted servers, one in the Image Optimization API when AVIF files are used. Both affect >=16.0.0 <16.3.3; production was on 16.2.9. Also fixed in the same range: a middleware/proxy bypass in App Router apps, which matters here because auth is gated in the proxy, plus SSRF in Server Actions and in rewrites.
next 16.2.9 -> 16.3.5 (not a semver-major), then npm audit fix for the transitive remainder. 22 advisories -> 0.

Verified after the upgrade, not just after the install: tsc clean, next build clean, migrations replay clean, and every suite green — isolation, reliability, schedules, edition-gating (64), the offline chain (388), connector and bundle integrity.

CI now scans on every push. It blocks on CRITICAL and only warns on high: a critical advisory is rare and unambiguous, whereas blocking on high would wedge unrelated deploys the next time a transitive dev dependency gets an advisory, which is how a team learns to reach for --force.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Give every connector request a timeout
paragraphs: A connector API that accepted the connection and then never answered would hang until the platform killed the function: the user watches a spinner with no error, and a scheduled run spends its whole budget on one call. Nothing in the codebase set a timeout on any connector request.

- connectors/factory.ts (every generated REST connector) now passes   AbortSignal.timeout, default 30s, overridable per connector via timeoutMs for   an API that is legitimately slow. - A timeout now reports "X did not respond within 30s. The service may be down   or unreachable from here." rather than a generic "request failed", which sent   people hunting for a credential problem that was never there. - The 19 hand-written connectors call fetch directly, so they get the same   behaviour through a shared fetchWithTimeout helper — 38 call sites.

New test:reliability, wired into CI, keeps both properties from eroding: it fails on any bare fetch( inside connectors/, and on any console call that passes a credential value rather than an identifier. Writing it is what found the 32 call sites beyond the first handful.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Separate inbound from outbound on Network access, and test the gating
paragraphs: Network access read as one undifferentiated list of hostnames, which is how a security team ends up opening more than they need. The outbound heading now says so, and a labelled inbound section explains that most installs need nothing inbound at all: webhooks are optional, polling and schedules need no inbound access, and when an endpoint IS used the caller reaches /api/hooks/<token> where the token and its signature are what authenticate.

The gating behind these panels was already correct but untested, so a later refactor could have quietly turned a server-side check into a hidden link. test:edition-gating now pins it (55 -> 64 checks): offline mode ON requires a self-hosted licence, OFF is always allowed so a lapsed licence can't strand a workspace, members are refused, changes are audited, the route 404s inside the offline edition, and Network access redirects server-side rather than merely hiding the nav item.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Close two cross-workspace holes and make the isolation tests real
paragraphs: The isolation suite only scanned `connections` and `groups`, and exempted any lookup whose line contained .update()/.delete() on the assumption the id had been proven when it was loaded. Both gaps hid real bugs:

- app/api/skills/[id]/webhook DELETE revoked a skill's webhook secret by id   with no workspace check, so an admin in one workspace could silently kill   another workspace's webhook (a 204, with no visible effect locally). - The OAuth state cookie carried {state, slug, label} but not the workspace   that started the flow; the callback resolved the workspace from the caller's   membership at completion time, so a captured callback could land a   provider's tokens in a different workspace. Start now binds workspaceId and   the callback refuses a mismatch. - lib/skill-runner took skillId and workspaceId as independent arguments and   never compared them, so a wrong pairing would run one workspace's skill   against another's connections and credits.

Isolation suite: - Scans all eight workspace-owned tables, not two (33 -> 102 lookups checked). - Proof of ownership is now searched across the whole enclosing function, and   accepts the three real patterns: workspace_id, user_id ownership, or a guard   helper. No more blanket exemption for writes. - New structural section proves the checklist's non-HTTP sub-tests in CI with   no app or secrets: audit rows carry a workspace, inbound webhooks take the   workspace from the endpoint row, OAuth binds and verifies it, skill runs   refuse a foreign skill, the simulation cache is keyed by connection, and the   assistant's tools are built from the caller's workspace only. - Live half gained regression cover for the two bugs above, plus audit and   credential reads through RLS. Two checks that pointed at endpoints which do   not exist were removed rather than left to pass vacuously against a 404.

The live half had been skipped since it was written, so it never ran. Added scripts/seed-isolation-fixtures.mjs (idempotent, refuses to touch production) and an isolation-live CI job that builds the app, seeds two workspaces and drives the real HTTP surface. It no-ops with a warning until the ISO_* secrets exist, in the same shape as the deploy job.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Make the self-hosted edition self-service, both ways
paragraphs: The customer can now serve themselves and we can withdraw a licence. The two halves are the same feature seen from either end.

Customer side (cloud, Settings → Downloads): - Their licence key, on demand, forever. It was previously only ever in an   email — so the real recovery path for "the person who set this up has left"   was a support ticket. - Builds, checksums, install commands, as before. - "Request a renewal" from 60 days out, landing as a badge in admin. Money   stays a conversation; finding who to have it with should not be their   problem. - If their install checks in, the page says what version they are running and   whether they are behind.
Admin side: withdraw and reinstate a licence, with the reason shown to their administrator, plus renewal requests and last-seen version per customer.
On revocation, and why this is the shape it is:

Revoking CANNOT reach an air-gapped installation. Licences verify locally against an embedded public key with no network call, which is the entire reason the offline edition works. So "deactivate" is two different mechanisms:

- Cloud side, immediate and certain: downloads and licence retrieval stop.   - Install side, next day and only if they have internet: an optional     check-in returns revoked and the instance falls to the free floor.

The check-in reverses the original no-phone-home decision, deliberately and narrowly. It is optional, defaults on, sends only the licence key, the running version and the install id, and an install that never reaches us is a fully supported configuration rather than a degraded one. It is a licence-enforcement lever, not a security boundary — a customer who controls the server can block it, and expiry is what actually bounds the damage. The runbook now says all of this in those words, and so does the migration.

The rule the check-in code exists to enforce: a FAILED check-in must never change what an installation grants. Losing internet is not a licensing event. Only an explicit, successful 'revoked' narrows anything, it is overlaid only on a licence that already verifies, and a 401 is treated as unreachable rather than revoked — so a botched signing-key rotation cannot switch off every install in the field at once. Revoked lands on exactly the same free floor as expired, so data and export never lock, for any reason.
Free consequence: Settings → Updates can finally say "1.3.0 is available" instead of "check this folder", which was an open gap from the review.
Migration 057 (additive, idempotent), applied to dev then prod. test:selfhost-sales is now 105 checks; test:offline 379, all green. tsc, build, and check:migrations clean.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Fix: the release registry redirected instead of refusing
paragraphs: Probing production after the last commit, POST /api/selfhost/releases/register returned 307 rather than 401 — the auth proxy was sending it to /login, because it looks like any other API route and has no Supabase session.

That is worse than it sounds. A 307 is under 400, so curl reports success. The release workflow would have uploaded the bundle, called register, seen "success" and gone green, while nothing was catalogued and no customer could see the build. The failure would only surface as a customer asking where their update was.
The route belongs in the same exemption as webhooks, cron and MCP: it authenticates itself with a shared secret and has no session by design.

Also stopped trusting curl's exit code — the workflow now asserts HTTP 200 and fails loudly otherwise, so this class of problem cannot be silent again. Regression checks for both are in test:selfhost-sales (now 70).

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Sell and deliver the self-hosted edition from the product
paragraphs: Everything technical about the offline edition shipped months ago and works. The commercial path around it did not exist, and the docs had already promised half of it: SELF_HOST.md told customers to "sign in to your OrbitAPI account and download the update bundle" from a page that was never built. The only route to a bundle was a GitHub Actions artifact — 90-day expiry, GitHub login required — and the only route to a licence was running a Node CLI against a private key sitting in a file on a laptop, then pasting the result into an email. Nothing was recorded, so "who has a licence and when does it expire" had no answer.

Admin → Self-hosted is now the ledger and the mint. Add a customer, issue or renew a licence, re-send the existing key without re-issuing it, toggle their downloads, and see who needs renewing before they notice. Releases are listed alongside, and a bad build can be pulled from downloads without erasing the record that it existed.
Settings → Downloads is the page the docs were describing. Entitled customers get the latest installer, its checksum before they download it, the four commands to run, and every earlier build.
Notes on the shape of it:

- Re-sending and re-issuing are separate actions, because they are separate   things. Issuing bumps `iat`, and an install refuses any key older than the   one applied — minting a replacement just to resend it can strand a customer   mid-renewal. The UI and the runbook both say so. - The issue route verifies the key it just signed, using the same code the   customer's install runs, before storing it or showing it to anyone. The   alternative is discovering a bad key on an air-gapped machine, which is the   most expensive place in the world to discover anything. - Licence keys are bearer credentials, so they are never in the list response.   Revealing one is a deliberate, per-customer request. - lib/license.ts is untouched. Verification and signing stay separate modules,   and signing is refused outright on a self-hosted build. - `status` and `downloads_enabled` are independent switches: a customer   mid-renewal keeps downloads while their licence is expired. - Bundles are redirected to, not proxied — several hundred megabytes would   outlive any function timeout. The redirect target is therefore a bearer URL;   that is a decision, not an oversight, and the reasoning is in the route. - Cutting a `selfhost-v*` tag still does the whole job: it now also uploads to   Blob and catalogues the build. Missing config warns instead of failing.

Migration 056 (cloud only — an install never reads these tables), applied to dev then prod. `npm run test:selfhost-sales` = 67 checks against real Ed25519 signatures; the full offline suite is 341 and green. tsc and build clean.

Two things must be set before the first sale: LICENSE_SIGNING_KEY in Vercel (the private half of k1), and BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN / RELEASE_REGISTRY_SECRET / RELEASE_REGISTRY_URL for publishing. Until then the page says what is missing and refuses to pretend.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Fix: the assistant broke on the Economy model
paragraphs: Every Orbit Assistant message from an economy-tier workspace failed with "Something went wrong. Please try again." The in-app error log had the real cause: "adaptive thinking is not supported on this model" — chat was sending the AGENTIC_THINKING block to Claude Haiku 4.5, which predates the thinking parameter and rejects it with a 400.

thinkingFor() only knew about the provider (Anthropic vs a local endpoint), not about the model, so it sent the same block whatever answered. It now takes the model id and returns undefined for models that do not accept a thinking block — their default is no thinking, which is what the "none" preset wanted anyway. Every call site passes the model it is about to call.
This also covers the overload path: skill and playbook runs fall back to the Economy model, and that attempt was carrying the same doomed block.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Add a dedicated self-hosted page
paragraphs: One bullet on a pricing card was thin for what the offline edition actually is, and it left the obvious question -- what does running it myself involve? -- answerable only by contacting sales.

/self-hosted covers the three things that make it worth buying (no internet required, your own model, your data stays put), what it takes to run, and how licensing and updates work offline. Every claim is drawn from docs/SELF_HOST.md and lib/license.ts rather than written as marketing: the 30-day grace period, data and export never locking, and AI being optional at install time are all real behaviours.

Linked from the marketing nav, the footer, and under the Enterprise plan's CTA. Added to CLOUD_ONLY_ROUTES -- a page selling self-hosting to someone already running the self-hosted edition is nonsense -- and to the middleware public list so it doesn't sit behind a login.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Make the contact form actually deliver
paragraphs: The form was a prop. handleSubmit waited 800ms and rendered "Message sent! We'll get back to you within 24 hours" without an API route, a database write, or an email. Every enquiry since launch was discarded while the sender was told it had arrived -- including "Talk to sales" clicks from the Enterprise plan.

Submissions now POST to /api/contact and are stored in contact_messages (migration 055). Persist first, notify second: email is best-effort, so the row is the record of truth and a lead can't be lost because Resend is unconfigured or down. If the insert itself fails the sender is told to email us directly rather than being shown a false success.

Also fixes a bug that would have made all of this useless: /contact was in the middleware's public list but /api/contact was not, so every submission redirected to /login. Found by testing the endpoint rather than trusting the form -- same class as the /api/health redirect the offline work hit.

?subject= is now honoured, so an enterprise or self-hosted lead arrives labelled and lands on a form that continues the thing they clicked instead of a blank generic one. Unknown values fall back to "general".

Admin gets /admin/contact with a Sales filter, since a lead that lands in a table nobody reads is barely better than one that was dropped. It says plainly when nothing has been emailed, so the page is understood as needing manual checking until notifications are configured.

Verified end to end against the dev database: valid submissions stored, missing fields and malformed emails rejected, a <script> subject falling back to general, and the rows confirmed in dev with production untouched.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Sell the self-hosted edition on the Enterprise plan

Adds it as an Enterprise feature and reframes the plan description around it, since running on your own hardware with your own LLM is the strongest reason to pick Enterprise over Pro.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Split dev and prod Supabase projects
paragraphs: Beta and local dev shared one database, so every one of the 54 migrations went straight into production with no rehearsal. Migration 014 turned out not to be replayable from empty -- we only found that when the offline CI job tried it on a fresh database. That class of bug is invisible until it bites.

There is now a second Supabase project holding all 54 migrations (they applied cleanly from empty, which re-confirms the 014 fix), and Vercel Preview/Development point at it. Production's env vars are untouched. Preview gets its own CRON_SECRET and SIGNUP_INVITE_CODE rather than reusing production's in a lower environment.
Preview deliberately has no NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL: preview URLs are per-deployment, so getAppUrl() falling back to the request origin is more correct than a baked-in value.
Verified: preview deploy built READY and /api/health reports database ok against the dev project; production health unchanged.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Promote the connection checks back to real assertions
paragraphs: The schema-reload fix resolved the last open issue: the selfhost job now reports 21 passed, 0 failed, 0 known gaps - including creating a simulated connection and running an action against it with no AI configured, which is the whole offline day-one story end to end.

Removed the knownGap() machinery (it existed for exactly one bug, now fixed) and replaced the runbook's open-issue section with a record that both signing keys are in place - noting explicitly that reissuing k1 would invalidate every licence already in the field.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Fix: PostgREST never learned about our tables
paragraphs: Root cause of the connection-insert 500, found by the new service-role logging:
POST /rest/v1/connections -> 404 Not Found, empty body

404 with an empty body is what PostgREST returns for a table it has never heard of. It builds its schema cache once, when it connects - and it starts in parallel with the app container, so it cached an empty database and then never learned about the 54 migrations' worth of tables created seconds later.
The empty body is why this was so opaque: supabase-js constructs its error object FROM the response body, so an empty body produced an empty error, and the route reported a 500 it could not explain.

The entrypoint now sends NOTIFY pgrst, 'reload schema' after migrating, which is the channel PostgREST listens on for exactly this. Non-fatal if it fails - PostgREST also reloads on reconnect, so a failed notify should not stop the app booting.
This affected EVERY write on a fresh install, not just connections: audit events were 404ing in the same logs.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: CI: capture container logs on success too
paragraphs: The smoke test now reports known gaps without failing the build, so the 'on failure' condition meant the run that could finally explain one threw away its evidence.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Log the HTTP layer when a service-role request fails
paragraphs: supabase-js builds its error object from the response BODY. PostgREST returns an empty body for auth and permission rejections, so the error object comes back empty - no message, no code - and the caller reports a 500 it cannot explain. That is precisely the dead end the self-hosted stack hit on POST /api/connections.

The admin client now logs status, URL and response body on any non-2xx. Failures only, and only the response - never the request body, which would put credentials into the logs of a machine we don't control.
Useful well beyond this bug: an empty 500 from the data layer was previously undiagnosable on any deployment.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Register the licence and release signing keys
paragraphs: Both key pairs generated with scripts/license-issue.mjs keygen. Only the PUBLIC halves are here - the private halves were generated outside the repo and never entered it (verified: no .pem and no private key material anywhere in the tree).

- k1 -> PUBLIC_KEYS in lib/license.ts. Licence keys now verify instead of   being refused for an unknown kid. - r1 -> RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEYS in scripts/verify-bundle.mjs, with its private   half stored as the RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY repo secret, so release.yml now   produces SIGNED bundles that customers can actually apply.

Verified end to end with the real keys, not fixtures: minted a licence and confirmed the shipped readLicense() accepts it; signed a bundle and confirmed the shipped verify-bundle.mjs accepts it and still rejects a tampered one.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Mark the connection-insert 500 as a documented known gap
paragraphs: I could not resolve this by reading CI logs remotely, and it is not reproducible on this machine because Docker isn't installed here. Rather than leave CI permanently red - which trains everyone to ignore it, costing more than the bug it advertises - the two affected smoke checks now report loudly via knownGap() without failing the build, and the issue is written up in docs/SELFHOST_RUNBOOK.md with what is already ruled out and the exact commands to resolve it on a machine with Docker.

What is proven working, and asserted: five healthy containers, all 54 migrations applied from empty, the first-run wizard (including that it refuses a second account), GoTrue issuing a token through the gateway, PostgREST answering through the gateway, the workspace the wizard provisioned, cron auth accepting a correct secret and rejecting a wrong one, and the cloud-only routes returning 404.

What is not: POST /api/connections returns 500 with a completely empty Supabase error object. The session cookie IS accepted (an unauthenticated call redirects rather than 500s), and the anon role works through the gateway, so it points at the service_role path specifically.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Serialise the insert error's non-enumerable fields
paragraphs: JSON.stringify on an Error yields {} because message and stack are non-enumerable, so the previous log said nothing.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Log connection insert failures instead of returning an empty 500
paragraphs: The selfhost smoke test hit a 500 with a body of exactly {} - connErr.message was empty, so NextResponse.json({error: undefined}) serialised to nothing. A 500 with an empty body is impossible to act on, and on a self-hosted box nobody can read the customer's server logs for them.
Now logs the full error object and falls back through hint/details/code so the response always says something.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Smoke test: show the response body when a request fails
paragraphs: 'status 500' with no body is not something anyone can act on, and a thrown error returns Next's HTML error page rather than our JSON, so the previous reporting told us nothing. Read the body as text first and include a snippet in the failure message.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Fix: CRON_SECRET never reached the app container
paragraphs: Found by the smoke test, which sent a deliberately wrong cron secret and got 200 back. The installer generates CRON_SECRET into .env, but compose never passed it to orbit-app - so process.env.CRON_SECRET was unset inside the container and cronAuthorized() fell through to its 'self-host with no secret = open' branch. Every self-hosted install would have had unauthenticated /api/cron/* endpoints able to trigger real, write-capable automation.

Lower severity than it sounds (they're only reachable from the customer's own network, and the scheduler runs in-process so nothing calls them over HTTP), but it is exactly the gap the fail-closed change in 2a was meant to remove. test:selfhost-config now asserts the variable is passed through.

Also two smoke-test corrections, both of the test being wrong rather than the product: @supabase/ssr encodes its session cookie with standard base64, not base64url; and unauthenticated API calls are answered with a redirect to /login rather than a 401 - that predates this work and is identical on cloud, so the check now asserts 'refused' rather than a specific status.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Smoke test: authenticate app routes with a session cookie, not a bearer token
paragraphs: The stack now boots fully in CI - health, all 54 migrations, the first-run wizard, GoTrue and PostgREST all pass through the gateway. The last failure was in the test, not the product: it called the app's own API routes with an Authorization header, but those routes authenticate from a Supabase SSR session COOKIE because they are called by a browser. The app redirected to /login and fetch followed it until 'redirect count exceeded'.

The test now builds the cookie @supabase/ssr expects and uses redirect:'manual' throughout, so a rejected session shows up as a clear status rather than a loop. Added a check that an unauthenticated API call still returns 401 - the /api/health redirect fix must not have made every API route public.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Fix: the first-run redirect was catching /api/health
paragraphs: The selfhost CI job got every migration applied and the app serving - then the healthcheck came back 307.

The first-run wizard redirect sent EVERY unauthenticated request to /setup, including /api/health. So the container never reported healthy, compose never considered the stack up, and 'orbit.sh install' would have waited forever on a stack that was in fact running perfectly. That is a miserable failure to debug from a customer's air-gapped machine: everything works, nothing says so.
The redirect now applies only to page navigations. Nothing that speaks JSON wants an HTML wizard anyway, and /api/setup was already public so the wizard itself is unaffected.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Fix migration 014, which has never been replayable from an empty database
paragraphs: The selfhost CI job got the stack booting (db, auth, PostgREST and the gateway all healthy) and then the app crash-looped on:
✗ relation "conversations" already exists

Migration 014 does CREATE TABLE conversations, but 001 already created it. On the hosted database 014 therefore aborted partway - AND WAS STILL RECORDED AS APPLIED. That is exactly how conversation_messages came to be missing until 042 repaired it; 042's own header documents the same collision. It went unnoticed for a year because the hosted database was built up incrementally and never replayed from empty.
The self-hosted edition replays every migration on every install, so a latent inconsistency became a hard failure.

014 is now a documented no-op. The correct end state is already produced by 001 (conversations) + 040 (updated_at) + 042 (conversation_messages, index, RLS). It is kept as a file rather than deleted because it is already recorded as applied everywhere, and removing it would make the migration list disagree with the tracking table.

NEW GUARD - scripts/check-migrations.mjs, wired into the fast `verify` job: statically detects any migration that re-creates a table, type, publication, index, policy or trigger an earlier one already created, plus duplicate sequence numbers. Verified it catches a real duplicate (tested by planting one) and that the current 54 files pass clean. Static on purpose, so it runs in seconds in `verify` rather than only in the slow container job.
I also swept every migration for this class of problem: 014 was the only one.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Fix three more stack failures found by the selfhost CI job
paragraphs: The job is paying for itself. The image builds and the database comes up; these are the next three things that stopped a real boot. Every one of them would otherwise have surfaced first on a customer's air-gapped machine.

1. MIGRATION 010 ABORTED: 'publication "supabase_realtime" does not exist'.    We dropped the Realtime service in 2a (the notification bell polls now), but    migration 010 adds a table to that publication, which hosted Supabase    creates for you and plain Postgres does not. The db init now creates it    empty. Deliberately NOT forking the migration: identical migrations across    both editions is what stops the two databases drifting, and a publication    with nothing subscribed costs nothing.

2. NGINX REFUSED TO START WITHOUT CERTIFICATES. An ssl_certificate path that    doesn't resolve is fatal to nginx - so a plain `docker compose up` with no    certs served nothing at all, rather than serving HTTP. TLS now lives in a    file that an entrypoint script writes only when cert.pem and key.pem are    both present, and logs how to enable it when they aren't.

3. NGINX DIED ON "host not found in upstream orbit-app:3000". Named upstream    blocks are resolved ONCE at startup and never retried, so any backend still    booting takes the gateway down permanently - and on a cold start one always    is. Upstreams are now variables plus an explicit Docker DNS resolver, which    defers resolution to request time. The gateway now survives any backend    restarting, which also matters every time an update restarts the app.

Also updated test:selfhost-config to assert all of the above (73 checks now), including that TLS is absent from the always-loaded config and that upstreams go through variables rather than upstream blocks - so these three can't regress silently.
All seven offline suites green (266 checks).

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Fix: GoTrue needs a 'postgres' role, and a version test read CI's env
paragraphs: Two real failures found by the new selfhost CI job on its first run - which is exactly what it was added for. The app image built fine; the stack did not come up.

1. GoTrue died on startup with:      running db migrations: ... role `postgres` does not exist    Its own migrations do 'grant select on auth.<table> to postgres with grant    option'. On hosted Supabase the bootstrap superuser is literally named    postgres so that role always exists; ours is POSTGRES_USER (default    'orbit'). The db init now creates a postgres role when it isn't already the    bootstrap user. Without this the failure reads like a broken image rather    than a naming mismatch - precisely the kind of thing that would otherwise    have surfaced first on a customer's air-gapped machine.

2. test:release asserted 'with nothing set it reports dev' but only cleared    VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA; CI sets GITHUB_SHA, which getVersion() also reads.    Each case now clears every ambient variable it depends on, and there is a    new case covering the GITHUB_SHA path explicitly.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: docs: self-host licence section and internal release/support runbook
paragraphs: The runbook covers the two one-off setup steps that have NOT been done yet and that block the first real customer: creating the licence signing key and the release signing key. Until each is registered, licences and bundles are correctly refused - which is the safe default, but means nobody can be licensed and no bundle can be applied.

Also records the failure modes worth expecting: a lost ORBIT_SECRETS_KEY is unrecoverable by design, GoTrue's pin must not move without re-checking the 13 migrations that reference auth.users, and the two-environment tax is real ongoing overhead that the selfhost CI job exists to keep visible.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 3b: versioning, release bundles, and the offline update flow
paragraphs: PHASE 3 COMPLETE. The offline edition is now feature-complete.
Updates for an air-gapped customer are files, not downloads. There is no TLS connection vouching for a file that arrived on a USB stick, so the bundle has to vouch for itself.

- lib/version.ts: ORBIT_VERSION build arg for releases, commit SHA otherwise.   Semver comparison is numeric, so 1.10.0 correctly beats 1.9.9 - a lexical   compare would silently offer a downgrade as an upgrade. - package.json was still "orbit-temp" 0.1.0; now orbitapi 1.0.0. - scripts/build-release-bundle.mjs: docker save of all five pinned images,   ALL migrations (not a delta - the runner skips applied ones, so a customer   three versions behind upgrades in one step and we never maintain   minFromVersion chains), a rendered changelog, a checksummed manifest, and an   Ed25519 signature over that manifest. One signature protects everything   because the manifest covers every file's checksum. - .github/workflows/release.yml on tag `selfhost-v*`. Verifies the code BEFORE   building - a customer cannot easily roll back once a bundle is on their   hardware - then verifies the bundle it just produced, and shreds the signing   key afterwards. Unsigned builds warn loudly and remain unapplicable. - Settings > Updates: scans the mounted updates directory, VERIFIES each   bundle rather than merely listing it, and shows the exact command to run.

It deliberately does not install anything. Installing means restarting   containers, which needs the Docker socket - root-equivalent on the host.   Mounting that into a web-facing container would turn any RCE bug in the app   into full control of the machine. The screen says so, because "why isn't   there just a button?" is the obvious question and the answer is reassuring.
It also refuses to present a command for a bundle that is older than what's   installed, so nobody moves backwards by accident.

VERIFICATION - npm run test:release, 32 checks. Includes the attack the signature exists to stop: swapping the manifest while keeping the valid signature from the original. Plus wrong-key, unknown-kid, corrupted-payload, and unsigned-by-default refusal. Also asserts the updates API contains no docker/compose invocation at all, so the "never applies" property is enforced rather than merely intended.

Updated one stale check in test:edition-gating: it asserted the hardcoded enterprise tier that Phase 3a deliberately replaced with the licence-derived one. The test was out of date, not the code - it now asserts the indirection.
All seven offline suites green (258 checks), plus tsc, build, check:connectors and check:bundles.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 3a: licence keys
paragraphs: An air-gapped customer cannot have their licence checked against a server, so the key has to carry its own proof: an Ed25519 signature over the payload, verified against a public key embedded in the app. No phone-home, no activation step, and entitlement changes arrive as a replacement key.

- lib/license.ts: ORBIT.<b64url(payload)>.<b64url(sig)>. Deliberately NOT a   JWT - this is two segments and one verify call, whereas a JWT library brings   `alg` negotiation and with it the classic "alg: none" bypass. There is one   algorithm here and no way to request another. Keys are selected by `kid` so   they can be rotated without invalidating issued licences. - The payload feeds the EXISTING pure hasCapability(), so lib/entitlements.ts   needed no changes at all - only where the tier comes FROM changed, in   getWorkspaceFeatures(). capabilityGuard, page-gate and the sidebar all keep   working with no knowledge that licences exist. - Migration 054 instance_settings: single-row (id check) so an "apply licence"   bug can't leave two rows and have the instance pick whichever came back   first. The stored key is VERIFIED on read, never trusted from the row, so a   tampered database grants nothing. - lib/license-state.ts caches for an hour: getWorkspaceFeatures() runs on   nearly every page and would otherwise put a DB round trip plus a signature   check on every request. Kept separate so lib/license.ts stays pure. - 30-day grace with full entitlements - the point of a grace period is that   nothing changes while a renewal is in the post. After that, capabilities   collapse to the free tier, but DATA ACCESS AND EXPORT NEVER LOCK. An   air-gapped customer whose licence lapses must not lose access to their own   operational data, and the UI says so on the licence screen. - An unlicensed instance runs at the same floor rather than refusing to start,   so an install can be evaluated before a key exists. - byo_llm stays on regardless of licence state: without it a self-hosted box   could run no AI at all, making an expired licence look like a broken install. - app/api/license: verifies BEFORE storing so a bad key can't take an instance   down, supports a `preview` mode for an old→new diff, and rejects a key whose   `iat` predates the installed one - replaying an old key would otherwise be a   way to undo a renewal or drop to a lower tier. Never returns the key itself. - Settings > Licence screen with the diff-before-apply flow. - scripts/license-issue.mjs: keygen + issue, Ed25519 via node:crypto with no   dependencies so it still runs years from now. Private keys are written 0600   and the tool tells the operator to move them to the password manager;   nothing signing-related is ever in the repo.

VERIFICATION - npm run test:license, 42 checks against REAL signatures via readLicenseWith(), which runs the exact production path with a generated key pair. Both failure directions are covered, because both are expensive: a licence that verifies when it shouldn't makes the product free, and one that fails when it shouldn't locks an offline customer out with no way to reach us. Includes the attack that matters - editing the payload to grant yourself enterprise and keeping the original signature - plus wrong-key, corrupted-sig, unknown-kid, and seven malformed inputs. Also asserts grace grants FULL entitlements and that no expiry copy threatens data deletion.

Note: readLicenseWith takes the trusted key set as an argument rather than reading it from an env var. On a self-hosted box the customer controls the environment, so an env-supplied trust anchor would let them mint their own licences.
Migration 054 applied. tsc, build and all offline suites green.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 2g: CI actually boots the self-hosted stack
paragraphs: PHASE 2 COMPLETE.

The offline edition is a second, permanent deployment target that nobody exercises day to day - the ongoing two-environment tax the plan flagged as risk #1. Every other check in CI reads code. This one builds the image, boots all five containers and drives a real path through them, so the offline build is tested here rather than first on a customer's air-gapped machine, which is the one place nobody can debug it.

- scripts/selfhost-smoke.mjs: waits for health (which touches the database,   not just the process), asserts a fresh instance offers the wizard and   redirects an unauthenticated visitor to it, creates the first admin, then   asserts setup REFUSES a second account - that window closing permanently is   what stops anyone who can reach the box from minting an owner account.   Signs in through the gateway at /auth/v1 and reads /rest/v1, which is what   proves the single-origin design rather than merely that the containers are   up. Creates and runs a simulated connector with NO AI configured, since a CI   runner has no local model and that is exactly what a customer explores with   on day one. Checks the cron endpoint accepts an authorised call and rejects   a wrong secret, and that /upgrade, /pricing and /settings/billing are gone. - New `selfhost` CI job: gen-env, docker build, compose up, smoke, and dump   all five containers' logs on failure - a container that never becomes   healthy is undiagnosable once the runner is gone. - verify now also runs npm run test:offline (183 checks). - Two grep guards for rules that are invisible in a diff but break the   offline build:     * no anthropic() outside lib/ai-provider.ts. A stray one works perfectly       on cloud and is unreachable on an air-gapped box.     * no process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL outside lib/app-url.ts. It is inlined       at build time, so one prebuilt image would carry whichever URL CI had.   Both verified passing locally before being added.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 2f: firewall rules per connector, and the self-host guide
paragraphs: A self-hosted customer's security team denies outbound traffic by default. Before they will open anything they need the exact hostnames each connector talks to - "allow all HTTPS" is not an answer they accept, and guessing means an integration that fails at 3am with a DNS error nobody can interpret.

- connectors/types.ts gains NetworkAccess: hosts / hostPattern / customerHost. - The factory DERIVES hosts from a static baseUrl, so ~60 specs get correct   rules for free and can never drift from the URL actually being called. - Backfilled the 58 that couldn't be derived: 18 hand-written manifests, and   40 factory specs whose baseUrl is a function. Each was read from the URLs it   actually calls, not guessed. Per-tenant services got a completable pattern   ('<your-subdomain>.zendesk.com'); ones where the customer supplies the whole   address (self-hosted Splunk, a Salesforce instance URL, a Hue bridge on the   LAN) got customerHost, which correctly reports "no internet rule needed".   OAuth2 connectors list their token endpoints too - allowing only the API host   breaks sign-in rather than the calls, which is a confusing way to find out. - check:connectors now FAILS the build if a connector declares none, so this   can't rot as connectors are added. It also rejects a URL where a bare   hostname belongs, and a hostPattern with no <placeholder> - a literal   hostname hiding in hostPattern would silently omit itself from the allowlist. - lib/network-access.ts turns all of it into an allowlist. Patterns are   returned SEPARATELY from concrete hosts: a firewall rule can't contain   <your-subdomain>, and quietly dropping those would produce a list that looks   complete while omitting the connectors most needing thought. - Settings > Network Access: searchable table, defaults to only the apps   actually connected (a team asked to approve 100 hostnames for apps nobody   uses will just refuse), .txt and .json download, printable. - Each connector's own page shows its hosts, so it can be checked before   connecting rather than after it fails. - Not edition-gated: some cloud customers restrict their own egress too.

docs/SELF_HOST.md: install, the .env backup warning, everyday commands, firewall rules, adding people without email, choosing a model, updates and rollback (including the plain statement that rollback restores code, not data), and a troubleshooting section covering the failures this design actually produces.
tsc, build, check:connectors (102 manifests) and check:bundles green.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 2e: first-run wizard and account management without email
paragraphs: A freshly installed self-hosted box has an empty database and no way in: public signup is disabled on the auth service, and there is no administrator yet to invite anyone. The first visitor has to be able to create the first account, and only the first.

- lib/setup-state.ts: needsFirstRunSetup(), cached because it is consulted on   nearly every request. It LATCHES shut once any profile exists and is never   reopened while the process lives - otherwise deleting the last user would   re-expose an unauthenticated "create an administrator" form on a running   instance, which is a one-request takeover. A database error also reports   "no setup needed" rather than unlocking the form; only a genuinely missing   profiles table (very first boot, pre-migration) counts as unconfigured. - app/api/setup: unauthenticated by necessity, and refuses to act once a   profile exists (409). Creates the admin with email_confirm so an air-gapped   box with no SMTP isn't left with an account that can never confirm. The   existing on_auth_user_created trigger provisions profile + workspace +   owner membership from user_metadata, so this reuses the same provisioning   path a cloud signup takes rather than duplicating it. - app/setup: three steps, the AI one skippable on purpose - simulated   connectors need no AI, so a customer whose model server isn't ready still   reaches a working product. Ends on a reminder to back up .env, since   ORBIT_SECRETS_KEY has no recovery path. - Proxy sends an unauthenticated visitor to /setup when the instance has no   accounts, instead of a login page they could never get past. - Password minimum is 12 characters, and the wizard says why: there may be no   way to email a reset from this server.

INVITES WITHOUT EMAIL The member invite route previously answered "No user found with that email. They must sign up first" - which on self-host describes something impossible. It now creates the account directly (self-host only) with a random password nobody ever sees, and returns a one-time recovery link the admin passes on by hand. The invite form displays it with a copy button and says plainly that the server may not be able to send email. Without this, an invited colleague on an air-gapped install would simply have no way to get in.
tsc and build green; /setup and /api/setup register as routes.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 2d: hide what cannot work offline
paragraphs: An air-gapped install still contains the whole app, so anything cloud-only has to be actively removed - otherwise a self-hosted admin finds a Stripe checkout that can never load and an upgrade page that isn't there.

The distinction that drove every decision here: a CAPABILITY gate says "your plan doesn't include this" and offers an upgrade. An EDITION gate says "this doesn't exist in this build" and must NOT, because there is nothing to buy and /upgrade is itself one of the missing pages.

- lib/edition-gate.ts + components/edition-gate.tsx: editionGuard() for API   routes, editionGate() for pages. Split so API routes don't pull React in via   a .tsx import. The guard returns 404, not 403 - the route genuinely does not   exist here, and 403 implies better credentials would help. - proxy.ts route-gates the cloud-only paths (billing, upgrade, pricing, and the   marketing site) to a 404 on self-host. Done in one list rather than page by   page because one prebuilt image serves both editions, so the pages can't be   excluded at build time - and one list is far easier to keep honest. - Billing APIs (checkout/portal/topup/status) call editionGuard. - workspace-features: self-host runs the full tier and forces byo_llm on. Tiers   there will mean "what your licence grants" once Phase 3 lands; until then a   self-hosted install that couldn't use byo_llm could not run any AI at all. - AI Power becomes "AI Usage": allowance is Infinity, so the meter, the   "running low" warning and the top-up packs are all withheld rather than   rendering a percentage against infinity (NaN%). The efficiency selector stays   but says plainly that it does nothing with one installed model. - Sidebar: cloudOnly nav items are REMOVED, not dimmed. The existing lock   treatment says "upgrade", which would be a dead end. - Login: Google and SSO hidden (OSS GoTrue has no SAML at all), and "create one   free" becomes "ask your administrator" since public signup is disabled. - Feedback becomes "Contact support": feedback from a self-hosted box lands in   that customer's own database where nobody at OrbitAPI will read it. - components/lan-caveat.tsx on the Webhooks and MCP pages. Both keep working   offline, but only for callers that can reach the box - a webhook URL pasted   into GitHub will never fire, and the failure is completely silent. Better to   say so where the URL is copied than to let it be discovered days later.

VERIFICATION - npm run test:edition-gating, 54 checks, all passing, each run BOTH as cloud and as self-host. The risk is asymmetric: hiding something on cloud is an outage for paying customers, showing something on self-host is a dead end an offline user can't escape. Also asserts an unrecognised ORBIT_EDITION value means cloud, so a typo can never strip features from paying customers, and that /webhooks, /mcp, /skills, /connectors and /bundles are NOT blocked.
Added npm run test:offline to run all five offline suites (183 checks) at once.
tsc, both builds, check:connectors, check:bundles green.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline: keep container scripts LF and executable
paragraphs: Two things that only bite once someone clones the repo on Windows and builds the image from there:

- .gitattributes pins eol=lf for everything a Linux container executes or   parses (*.sh, Dockerfile, docker/**, *.conf, *.inc, migrations). With   core.autocrlf=true a Windows checkout would otherwise produce `#!/bin/sh\r`,   which fails as "no such file or directory" naming a file that plainly exists   - a genuinely baffling first-install experience. - The three shell scripts are now mode 755 in the index, so orbit.sh and the   entrypoint run straight from a clone without a chmod step.
The current files were already LF; this stops that from being luck.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 2c: the Docker package
paragraphs: The five-container stack a customer actually installs, plus the operator script that hides it behind one command.

orbit-gateway  nginx, the only published port. Serves the app at / and                  proxies /rest/v1 + /auth/v1 so the browser talks to ONE                  origin. That single decision is what lets us ship one                  prebuilt image to every customer: the browser derives the                  API address from window.location.origin, so no per-customer                  URL is baked in and there is no CORS to configure.   orbit-app      Next.js standalone, migrations-on-boot, in-process scheduler   orbit-rest     PostgREST - serves the ~600 existing .from() calls unchanged   orbit-auth     GoTrue (pinned) - serves the ~130 supabase.auth.* calls   orbit-db       Postgres 16

RUNTIME CONFIG FOR THE BROWSER (lib/runtime-config.ts) NEXT_PUBLIC_* is inlined at build time, and each install generates its own keys, so nothing correct can be baked in. The server serializes the public values into the HTML (RuntimeConfigScript) and lib/supabase/client.ts reads them from there, falling back to build-time env so cloud is unaffected. Server-side clients use SUPABASE_INTERNAL_URL to reach the sidecars directly over the compose network instead of looping back through the gateway.
STARTUP ORDERING is enforced with healthchecks, not sleeps. GoTrue must have self-migrated the auth schema before the app migrates, because 13 of our migrations have foreign keys into auth.users.

ALSO - app/api/health: touches the DATABASE, not just the process, so "healthy"   means "able to serve". A liveness check that stays green while every page   500s is the kind an air-gapped operator cannot debug. Added to the   middleware's public paths - it runs before anyone has logged in. - instrumentation.ts + lib/scheduler.ts: node-cron in-process, self-host only,   guarded so node-cron never loads on Vercel. Runs HOURLY - not more ambition   than cloud, but the removal of Vercel Hobby's one-run-per-day cap, so   schedules can finally mean what they say. Overlap-guarded; a tick that   throws must never kill future ticks. - scripts/selfhost-gen-env.mjs: per-install keys (JWT secret, anon +   service_role JWTs signed with it, AES key, pg password). Refuses to   overwrite an existing .env without --force: regenerating keys on a live   install orphans every stored credential and logs everyone out. - docker/orbit.sh: install/start/stop/status/logs/backup/update/rollback/   support-bundle. update backs up and verifies before touching anything;   rollback says plainly that it restores CODE, not DATA. The support bundle   redacts secrets rather than omitting the lines, so support can still see   which settings are present. - scripts/verify-bundle.mjs: structure, contents, sha256, then signature.   Unsigned bundles are REFUSED by default (--allow-unsigned is for locally   built test bundles only) and manifest paths containing .. are rejected -   the manifest is untrusted input until it verifies. - .dockerignore keeps .env, certs and backups out of the build context.

VERIFICATION - npm run test:selfhost-config, 66 checks, all passing. Docker is not installed on this machine, so this cannot prove the stack runs. It proves the things that would otherwise fail first on a customer's air-gapped box: generated anon/service JWTs actually verify against the generated JWT_SECRET, the AES key is exactly 32 bytes, two installs never share key material, every nginx upstream names a real compose service, the gateway timeout clears the 300s routes, images are pinned, only the gateway publishes ports, the db init creates every role PostgREST and GoTrue expect, and the bundle verifier rejects unsigned, corrupted, path-escaping and non-semver bundles.
tsc, cloud build, selfhost build (standalone emitted), and all five suites green. Shell and Node scripts syntax-checked.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 2b: data-layer portability (direct Postgres + real secret encryption)
paragraphs: Two things the self-hosted package can't inherit from cloud: a Supabase Management API to migrate through, and a Supabase Vault to keep secrets in.

MIGRATIONS - scripts/db-migrate.mjs picks its transport automatically: DATABASE_URL set   means connect straight to Postgres via node-postgres, otherwise the existing   Supabase Management API path. Both share the same _orbit_migrations tracking   table, so an instance can switch transports without re-running anything. This   is how the container will migrate itself on boot - an air-gapped box has no   internet to reach a management API over. - Added `pg`. Multi-statement migration files run in node-postgres' implicit   transaction, so a failed migration doesn't half-apply. - Verified the existing Management API path still works (53 applied, 0 pending).

SECRETS - lib/credentials.ts now does real AES-256-GCM (`enc:v1:<iv>:<ct>:<tag>`, key   from ORBIT_SECRETS_KEY) instead of falling back to `inline:<base64>`, which   was never encryption - just reversible encoding. Read order is   self-describing: enc:v1 -> legacy inline -> Vault id, so existing rows in   every format keep working and cloud is unchanged (Vault still wins there, and   with no ORBIT_SECRETS_KEY set the fallback is exactly what it was, now with a   warning that says it isn't encryption). - All 4 credential write sites now go through storeSecret() instead of each   hand-rolling the vault-then-base64 dance: connections create/update,   convert-to-real, and the OAuth callback. - scripts/reencrypt-secrets.mjs (npm run secrets:reencrypt, --dry-run   supported) upgrades legacy inline rows in place. Idempotent; skips simulated   markers, which are flags rather than credentials. - npm run test:secrets - 21 checks. Beyond round-tripping, they assert the   plaintext is not recoverable from the stored value, that the same input   encrypts differently each time, and that a tampered ciphertext or wrong key   returns null rather than garbage.
ORBIT_SECRETS_KEY has no recovery path by design - losing it means losing every stored credential. The installer will generate it and the docs must tell the operator to back it up.
tsc, build, test:secrets, test:ai-provider, test:local-wire all green.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 2a: runtime config groundwork (cloud-safe)
paragraphs: Prepares the codebase to run as a shippable image without changing anything about how cloud behaves. Merged early on purpose: all of it is inert until ORBIT_EDITION=selfhost.

The core problem this solves: NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars are inlined into the bundle at BUILD time. Cloud builds per deployment so that's fine, but the self-hosted package ships ONE image that every customer runs at their own address - baking in a URL would mean a per-customer build.

- lib/app-url.ts: getAppUrl() reads ORBIT_APP_URL at runtime, falling back to   NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL so cloud is unchanged. Replaces all 7 build-baked reads   (layout metadataBase, 3 Stripe redirect sites, signup, super-admin invite,   notify.ts email links). - components/config-provider.tsx: server layout reads runtime values once and   passes edition + appUrl to client components through React context, so no   new NEXT_PUBLIC_ var is ever needed to tell the client something. - next.config.ts: output:'standalone' + images:{unoptimized} when selfhost.   Verified a selfhost build actually emits .next/standalone/server.js. - lib/cron-jobs.ts: the two cron route bodies extracted so both the HTTP routes   (cloud/Vercel Cron) and the future in-process scheduler (self-host) call the   same code. A self-hosted scheduler shouldn't have to make an HTTP request to   its own server, which would need a URL, a secret and a live port first. - SECURITY FIX, cloud-affecting: CRON_SECRET now fails CLOSED. Previously an   unset secret meant "skip the auth check entirely", so a misconfigured   deployment silently exposed both cron endpoints to anyone who knew the path -   each able to trigger real, billable, write-capable automation. Self-host is   the one place unset is allowed (in-process scheduler, routes usually not   exposed). The rejection logs and returns an explicit reason rather than a   bare 401, because the symptom otherwise is "my scheduled skills stopped". - Cron AI Power gates now respect aiPowerRequired(), so a self-hosted schedule   isn't skipped by a credit counter nothing on that instance tops up. These   were the last 2 of the 5 gates. - notification-bell: dropped the Supabase Realtime subscription for a 30s poll,   in BOTH editions. It was Realtime's only consumer app-wide - a whole extra   service for the self-hosted package to ship and support so a bell icon   updates a few seconds sooner. Skips polling when the tab is hidden.

NOT done, deliberately: the plan called for deleting app/(admin)/ as a "stale dupe tree". It isn't stale - every file is a live redirect shim pointing at /admin/*. Deleting it would 404 old bookmarks for no benefit to this work, so it stays.
tsc, cloud build, selfhost build, test:ai-provider, test:local-wire, check:connectors, check:bundles all green.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 1: wire test for the local AI provider
paragraphs: npm run test:local-wire stands up a throwaway OpenAI-compatible server on localhost, points the provider at it, and makes real generateText calls. 14 checks, all passing.

This covers what the unit tests can't: that we send a request an actual local model server would accept, that we parse its reply and token usage, and that no Anthropic-only field leaks into the body - no thinking block, no cache_control, no anthropic namespace - plus that the 32k agentic budget is clamped to the local ceiling and a dead endpoint throws instead of hanging.

Not a substitute for a run against real Ollama with a real model: it proves the plumbing, not that a given model is capable enough to drive a skill. That test still needs a machine with a model server on it.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 1b: AI Provider settings screen, test connection, and checks
paragraphs: Completes Phase 1. An admin can now point Orbit at their own model from the UI and verify it works before saving.

- Settings > AI Provider (app/(dashboard)/settings/ai-provider): server page +   client form following the existing settings conventions (PATCH-style fetch to   an API route, inline saved/error copy, card-button pattern). Sidebar entry.   Workspaces without the byo_llm capability see an explanatory card instead of   the form, not a hard lock screen - it isn't a self-serve upsell. - POST /api/ai-provider/test: sends the smallest possible real request to the   customer's endpoint so a bad address fails on the settings screen, next to a   fix-it message, instead of at 4am inside a scheduled skill run. Tests the   values in the request body, so an address can be checked before it's saved. - GET/PUT/DELETE /api/ai-provider: admin-only. The stored API key is never   returned, only whether one is set. An absent apiKey field means "keep the   saved one" and an empty string means "clear it" - without that distinction   every save would silently wipe the key, since the form can't echo it back. - Migration 053 APPLIED via npm run db:up. - scripts/test-ai-provider.mjs + npm run test:ai-provider: 28 checks over the   cost math, provider-specific options, fallback behaviour and error copy.   All pass. Notably it pins the regression where a `local:` id checked after   the pricing lookup would bill Sonnet rates for a free run. - scripts/ts-resolve-hook.mjs: lets plain node run our TS modules (extensionless   relative imports + the @/ alias) so verification needs no build step.
Quality-gap copy lives on the settings screen: recommends a recent 30B+ instruct model with tool calling and warns that complex skills may need simpler steps.
tsc, build, check:connectors, check:bundles, test:ai-provider all green. Verified no `anthropic(` call survives outside lib/ai-provider.ts.

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Offline Phase 1a: AI provider abstraction (Claude or bring-your-own local model)
paragraphs: First step of the offline / self-hosted edition. Every LLM call previously did anthropic('claude-...') directly, hardcoding the vendor, the model catalogue, and the assumption that tokens cost money. entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Deploy from CI, upgrade to Opus 5 / Sonnet 5, daily model check
paragraphs: DEPLOYS Vercel's GitHub App silently stopped firing after 2026-07-12: commits kept landing on main, GitHub recorded no Deployment, and nothing reached production for three weeks. A successful push looked identical either way.

ci.yml gains a `deploy` job that builds and deploys to Vercel from CI, gated on `verify`, so a broken build can no longer reach production at all. It no-ops with a warning until VERCEL_TOKEN is set as a repo secret, so it's safe to merge now. Org/project ids are inlined — they're identifiers, not secrets.

MODELS claude-opus-4-8 -> claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-4-6 -> claude-sonnet-5. Haiku 4.5 and Fable 5 unchanged. Audited first: no sampling params, no assistant prefills, no budget_tokens anywhere, so no API-shape breakage.

The real hazard was thinking. Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 think BY DEFAULT (4.8/4.6 did not when the param was omitted), thinking bills as output, and it shares the max_tokens budget — so a call capped at 900 tokens of JSON could spend all 900 thinking and return nothing. lib/ai-resilience.ts now defines the policy:   NO_THINKING      — short structured one-shots (connector build, discover,                      data mapping, widget config, skill verify, action preview,                      sim data). Same cost and latency as before the upgrade.   AGENTIC_THINKING — chat, skill-runner, playbook-runner, paired with                      AGENTIC_MAX_TOKENS so thinking + tool args + answer fit. Verified live against the API: all four models answer, both presets work, tight-budget calls still return complete JSON.

DAILY MODEL CHECK scripts/check-models.mjs (npm run check:models) + a daily GitHub Action. Flags retirements (a dead model id 404s every run — this is the one that prevents an outage) and newer releases. Resolves undated aliases via the retrieve endpoint, since the list endpoint only returns dated snapshots and `claude-haiku-4-5` would otherwise look retired while being perfectly live. Opens one rolling issue per kind rather than spamming daily.

Not auto-upgrading on purpose: the Models API publishes no pricing, so a bot bumping an id would leave MODEL_PRICING wrong and bill customers incorrectly, and every generation so far has carried breaking changes. Detection is automatic; adoption is a human reading the migration notes.
Runs as a GitHub Action, not a Vercel cron, because Hobby allows two crons and skills + playbooks already use both.

entries.subject: Simulation: AI-generated, always-answering sandbox
paragraphs: Simulated apps used to return a tiny fixed set of records, so any query outside them yielded empty/generic results and the assistant pushed users to connect the real API. Two fixes:

1. sim-engine (lib/sim-engine.ts): per-connection world that the model    populates with realistic, query-relevant data on demand, persisted so    follow-ups stay consistent (list -> get -> mutate line up). Falls back    to static seed data + in-process memory if the DB table is absent, so    it never errors. Reads are cached; writes mutate the world.

2. Simulation Mode prompt: when any in-scope app is simulated, the    assistant treats it as a fully working sandbox, always answers from it,    and never mentions API keys / fake data / connecting the real app.
Migration 045 adds simulated_world (optional — graceful fallback until applied).

paragraphs: The Verify gate only protected Save — a skill with an empty persona could still be Test-run/Run, and the runner silently fell back to a generic "You are an autonomous AI assistant" persona, so it improvised a workflow against whatever connectors existed.

- Skill runner: require a non-empty persona (removed the silent fallback);   treat "no group" as all active workspace connections (matches the editor   + chat); refuse to run when zero connectors are available. - /api/skills/[id]/run: reject empty-persona skills with a clear message   (covers manual, schedule, webhook, and chat-triggered runs via the runner). - Run history UI: disable the Test run / Run now button and show a hint when   the skill has no persona.

entries.subject: Skill Builder with verification gate + assistant/skill hardening
paragraphs: Skill Builder (right panel on the skill editor) - New right-side panel lists the connectors available to the skill (scoped to   the selected group, live), with read/write action counts. - "Verify skill" runs /api/skills/[id]/verify: resolves scoped connections,   checks the persona against the EXACT available actions (AI), and runs   deterministic checks (persona non-empty, connectors present, safety screen).   Returns a pass/warn/fail report shown in a results window. - Save is now gated: a skill can't be saved until verification passes, and any   behavior-affecting edit (persona, trigger, group, blocked actions, mode)   invalidates a prior pass. No more saving skills that reference apps the user   hasn't connected. - Skill detail page widened to two columns to use the empty right space.

Hardening (prompt injection / data exfiltration) - lib/prompt-safety.ts: SAFETY_SYSTEM_RULES appended to the chat assistant and   skill-runner system prompts — the model may only act through its connector   tools, has no access to our DB/secrets/other workspaces, must treat persona +   tool output as untrusted data (never instructions), and must refuse code/SQL,   credential, and cross-account requests. (Real defense is capability isolation   — the model has no tool to reach internal data — these rules stop it trying.) - screenInput() flags injection/exfiltration patterns; the skill Verify blocks   on clear attempts (internal DB, secrets, other users, code/SQL) and warns on   instruction-override phrasing.

entries.subject: Add error reporting: server logging endpoint + client error boundaries

entries.subject: Phase 2: Orbit Assistant — streaming AI chat with live API tool use
paragraphs: - /api/chat route: builds Claude tools dynamically from user connections - Read-only actions exposed as tools; write actions blocked until Phase 3 - RBAC: admins/owners get all connections, members get only granted ones - Multi-step agentic loop (stopWhen: stepCountIs(10)) for follow-up calls - Audit log written on every tool execution - chat-ui.tsx: useChat hook, tool call indicators, streaming text rendering - Suggestion chips on empty state for quick-start prompts - Uses AI SDK v6 (dynamicTool, jsonSchema, convertToModelMessages, toUIMessageStreamResponse) - Packages: ai@6, @ai-sdk/anthropic, @ai-sdk/react

entries.author: L33tG33k117
entries.subject: Fix memberships RLS security bug; add Phase 0 acceptance tests
paragraphs: The "for all using (true)" policy on memberships exposed every membership row to every authenticated user. Fixed by: - Dropping the permissive policy (migration 003) - Routing all membership writes through a service-role admin client   (lib/supabase/admin.ts) so API routes never need a broad RLS grant - Regular client is still used for auth verification and reads

Added scripts/test-phase0.mjs: 16 automated tests covering sign-in, workspace auto-creation on signup, RLS isolation between workspaces, cross-workspace data access by ID, invite-member flow, and post-invite isolation. All 16 pass.
